title: Business Holiday Cards: Who Gets One and What to Write Inside
excerpt: Who to send business holiday cards to, what to write inside, which card to pick and how early to order so they land before the holidays.
author: David Stein
featuredAlt: Folded cream holiday cards with pine branch and red berry corners, white envelopes and a fountain pen on a wood desk
content:
Send business holiday cards to the people who keep your business going: your best customers, the people who send you referrals, your key vendors and your own staff. Inside, write a short, warm note and sign it by hand. Leave the sales pitch out. Order early enough that you still have time to sign and mail them before the holidays, which for most businesses means placing the order in November.

I print custom business holiday cards in Columbus with your logo, a writable inside and envelopes to match. Below is how I'd build the list, what to put inside and how to plan the timing so the cards don't arrive in January.

Who gets a holiday card

Start with the people you'd thank in person if you had the time. For most small businesses that list looks something like this:

  • Customers who bought from you more than once this year.
  • Anyone who sent you a referral, whether they're a customer, a friend or another business.
  • Vendors and subcontractors you lean on, like your supplier rep or the electrician you call first.
  • Your staff and their families, especially the ones who worked the busy weeks.
  • Landlords, bankers, accountants and other people who make running the business easier.

A dental office might add the doctors who refer patients. A real estate agent might add every client who closed this year. A contractor might send one to each customer from the last season. You don't need a huge list. Runs start at 25 cards, so a short list of the people who matter most works fine.

What to write inside

Keep it short and personal. The printed message can be one line, like warm wishes for the holidays from all of us at your company name. The handwritten part is what people remember.

  • Use the person's first name.
  • Mention one specific thing, like the job you did for them, the referral they sent or the year you've worked together.
  • Sign it yourself. If several people sign, it reads like a team that knows them.
  • Leave out coupons, offers and requests for reviews. Save those for a postcard in January.

If your customers celebrate different holidays, a season's greetings or happy new year message works for everyone. A new year card also gives you a little more time if you're running late.

Picking the card

The 5 x 7 folded card is the classic holiday size. The 5.5 x 8.5 and 4.25 x 5.5 folded sizes are the other standard options, and each one has an envelope that fits.

Most people pick a glossy outside with an uncoated inside. The photo or design on the front looks sharp, and any pen writes clean on the inside without smearing. If you want the card to feel more special, raised foil, kraft paper or pearl paper all stand out on a desk.

Put your logo small on the back, not big on the front. A holiday card that looks like an ad gets treated like one. If you want your return address printed on the envelopes, my letterhead and envelopes page covers that.

How early to order

Work backward from when you want the cards to land. Then leave time for each step:

  • Pull together your list and addresses.
  • Send me your logo and message, and approve the proof.
  • Printing.
  • Signing and writing notes, which always takes longer than people expect.
  • Mailing, which slows down in December when everyone else is mailing too.

The signing step is the one that sinks most plans. If you have a long list, split it up among your team or sign a stack each morning. Ask me when you order and I'll tell you how long printing will take for your quantity and paper, so you can plan the rest.

Keep the list for next year

The hardest part of holiday cards is usually the list, not the card. Once you've pulled names and addresses together, save them in one place, like a spreadsheet or your customer software. Add a column for who signed and what you wrote. Next year you start with a list that's mostly done, and you won't send the same note twice.

While you're at it, fix the addresses that bounced back last year and add the customers and referral partners you picked up since. A clean list also makes it easy to send a thank-you card the moment someone sends you work.

Thank-you cards the rest of the year

Once the holiday rush is over, keep a box of thank-you cards at the front desk. A short note after a referral or a big job does the same work as a holiday card, and it shows up when nobody else is sending one. Many businesses order both at the same time so the design matches. For year-end mailers that do carry an offer, printed postcards are the better fit.
